Meeting header:
Date: 2028-07-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE); Priya Desai (Redwood SE); Asha Rao (Sandstone Head of AI); Mark Li (Sandstone CTO); Diego Fernandez (Eng Mgr)

Auto-generated summary: demo+strategy session; medium transcription quality; action items captured.

00:00 Jordan Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood Inference, i'm the AE on this account, with me is priya our se, we'll jump through a short overview of how JSON mode and typed payloads work in the console and then show the runtime fallbacks and a couple optimize recommendations.
00:18 Asha Rao: thanks jordan, excited — quick context, we're replacing some internal orchestration that does call routing and a light schema enforcement layer. concern is making sure we can keep latency under 250ms for our chat snippets and keep costs predictable.
00:35 Priya Desai: awesome, that helps. quick q: are you mostly hosted now or self-hosted? like do you call openai or run internal endpoints?
00:42 Mark Li: we're hybrid, majority calls go to a managed api right now but we also have an on-prem inference pipeline for sensitive data. so any solution that requires us to lift data out is harder.
00:55 Jordan Kim: got it, so data residency and private deployment are important. worth noting we offer hosted, dedicated pools, and private (v-p-c / on-prem) — there's also an option to have a private control plane.
01:10 Diego Fernandez: when you say private control plane — is that fully airgapped? we have a couple customers in healthcare that need near air-gap.
01:18 Priya Desai: short answer: we support tight network isolation, and an on-prem package that can be deployed with no egress to redwood telemetry if requested. we'll follow up with the exact steps — but folks often ask about KMS integration too.
01:34 Mark Li: right — so encryption at rest and using our KMS for keys is a must.
01:39 Jordan Kim: totally — we'll include notes on KMS/HSM in the security pack. also SOC 2 and audit logs are available, apologies if the ai transcriber says "sock two" in places, it sometimes does that.
01:50 Asha Rao: (laughs) i see that a lot.
01:55 Priya Desai: ok switching to the console demo — i'm going to share my screen, you'll see the models catalog and the JSON mode toggle. JSON mode lets you define a schema for the expected output, typed fields, and then the runtime enforces the schema and can do safe tool invocations.
02:15 (screen share begins — console UI noises)
02:32 Priya Desai: here i have a sample schema: a ticket object with id:string, severity: enum(low|medium|high), assignee:{name,email}, and an actions array. in the actions array we can declare allowed tool calls like lookup_user and create_jira_ticket. the runtime validates the model output and if it doesn't conform, the fallback can either attempt recovery, call a sanitizer tool, or return an error.
02:58 Asha Rao: how deterministic is the schema enforcement? like do we need a second pass with a parser model?
03:05 Priya Desai: good q — we do a primary enforcement step inside the runtime; if the model output deviates we have configurable fallback policies: auto-correct (with a small templated repair prompt), sandboxed re-invoke, or route to a deterministic parser. for high-assurance flows we recommend the auto-sanitize then deterministic parser fallback.
03:30 Jordan Kim: and you can tune that per-route; so chat endpoints can be lenient, while actions like billing or PII export would use strict enforcement.
03:42 Mark Li: what about tool calling safety? we can't allow arbitrary outbound calls.
03:48 Priya Desai: exactly — tool calling is sandboxed. the console lets you declare a set of callable tool schemas. at runtime the model can only produce action objects that match those schemas. anything outside is rejected. we also sign and log tool invocations and you can route them through a gateway inside your v-p-c.
04:10 Diego Fernandez: cool — and are those logs shipable to our SIEM? we already ingest into Splunk.
04:17 Jordan Kim: yes — audit logs can stream to your syslog/Splunk/CloudWatch. we'll include the log format in the security pack.
04:25 Priya Desai: jumping into a quick example — i'll trigger a flow that asks the model to extract entities and call lookup_user. watch the typed payload in the response pane.
04:40 (typing, short pause)
04:55 Priya Desai: ok you can see the model generated the action object with name:lookup_user and payload:{email: "alice@example.com"}. the runtime matched it to the lookup_user schema and executed the tool in a sandboxed environment; the tool returned a user_id and the runtime inserted that into the final response.
05:18 Asha Rao: does the runtime store kv cache for the user? we have long sessions and want to avoid repeated fetches.
05:25 Priya Desai: yes — the KV cache can cache prefixes and tool outputs. it's configurable with TTL, and you can define what keys are stored. note: caching reduces token usage but be mindful of PII retention policies.
05:40 Mark Li: ok latency question — with sandboxed tool calls and typed enforcement, what's the SLO impact?
05:48 Priya Desai: typical overhead is small — a few tens of milliseconds for schema validation; tool calls add the tool latency obviously. for tight 250ms SLOs we recommend a combination of model selection (smaller context model), local dedicated pools, and aggressive batching for non-interactive workloads. the console's Optimize tab will suggest batching and quantization profiles based on your request distribution.
06:15 Jordan Kim: also we have smart routing — you can route latency-sensitive traffic to dedicated low-latency capacity while routing bulk jobs to cheaper quantized endpoints.
06:28 Diego Fernandez: how granular is routing? can we route by customer tier or route by token-per-request?
06:34 Jordan Kim: yes — routes can be policy-driven: by api key, by route, by token cost, region, or custom tags.
06:42 (brief cross-talk)
06:50 Asha Rao: i want to dive into the Optimize recommendations after this.
06:55 Priya Desai: sure, i'll demo the Optimize tab in a bit. first i want to show schema drift detection — if your regular prompts start generating slightly different shapes, the console flags regressions against a baseline prompt set and shows token cost impact.
07:15 Mark Li: that's useful. how do you handle model rollouts? we can't have regressions slip into production.
07:22 Priya Desai: rollouts are built-in — you can do canary or A/B; if a model introduces schema regression, the system can automatically rollback to the previous variant. we tie quality regressions to a prompt test-suite so you get alerted immediately.
07:40 Diego Fernandez: what's the onboarding? we have a small infra team and a platform team — who owns the pilot?
07:48 Jordan Kim: pilots are typically AE+SE assisted for first 2 weeks; we help instrument the evals and advise on batch sizing/quantization. after that your platform team can take over.
07:58 Asha Rao: timeline expectation? we want this in production for a gated set of customers in 8 weeks if possible.
08:05 Jordan Kim: plausible — typical 4-week pilot then production rollout over 4–8 weeks depending on integration complexity. we'll scope concrete milestones in the pilot doc.
08:14 Priya Desai: now the Optimize tab — you can upload a sample of real requests and the optimizer gives recommendations: batch sizes, KV TTLs, model quantization levels. here i've uploaded a small sample and it's suggesting a 3x token reduction by enabling prefix caching and switching this route to an 8-bit quantized variant.
08:38 Mark Li: any quality delta with quantization? we need to make sure hallucinations don't increase.
08:44 Priya Desai: minor deltas for some models; Optimize simulates quality changes using held-out prompts and flags prompts where quantization causes a regression. we recommend running a short A/B for a subset of traffic.
08:58 Asha Rao: security again — SSO and RBAC are important. Can we map roles to allowed tool actions? we don't want support engineers to call billing tools.
09:08 Priya Desai: yes — RBAC is plumbed through SSO/SAML; you can map groups to allowed routes and to allowed callable tools. so role-based tool restrictions are possible.
09:20 Diego Fernandez: what about on-prem installation complexity? do we need to recompile anything?
09:26 Jordan Kim: no, the on-prem package is a docker/k8s helm chart with configurable kernel selection — the runtime picks kernels at startup. we provide an ops guide; for heavy optimization we can assist with a short services engagement.
09:40 (short pause)
09:48 Priya Desai: real world note — sometimes the transcriber hears "K-V cash" instead of KV cache, just so you know if you later search the transcript.
09:55 (laugh)
10:00 Mark Li: thanks. can you talk about GDPR/data residency? our eu customers require no cross-border transfer and log deletion on request.
10:09 Jordan Kim: for EU data you can deploy private control plane in eu regions, and logs can be retained in-region. we also offer configurable retention and deletion hooks for data subject requests. we'll include the legal data processing addendum.
10:24 Asha Rao: excellent. i want to test a conservative flow: schema enforcement + deterministic parser fallback + no outbound calls for certain routes. is that doable?
10:33 Priya Desai: absolutely — you can set a policy: strict enforcement, deterministic parse fallback, tool calls disabled. the console has a policy editor for that.
10:45 Diego Fernandez: one of our concerns: how are model variants named? devs maintain many models and we need stable versioning for experiments.
10:53 Priya Desai: models are versioned and you can pin by model id. rollouts and ABs reference model ids so devs get stable references. we also keep model artifacts in the catalog.
11:05 Jordan Kim: quick pause for questions.
11:10 Asha Rao: on the pilot, what metrics should we track as success criteria?
11:16 Priya Desai: recommended: avg latency (p95), token cost per 1k sessions, schema error rate, successful tool call rate, and customer-perceived correctness (from a human eval sample).
11:30 Mark Li: ok, those look good.
11:35 Diego Fernandez: any known limits on concurrent tool executions per route? we want to avoid throttles in peak.
11:42 Priya Desai: we surface concurrency limits per pool; dedicated pools are recommended for predictable throughput, and you can configure burst capacity. we'll include suggested pool sizing based on your traffic sample.
11:55 (screenshare: sample policies)
12:10 Priya Desai: demo wrap-up — i'll show a quick failure scenario: model returns malformed action, runtime runs sanitize policy and then re-invokes with a repair prompt. watch the logs — you'll see the sanitizer patch and an audit log entry.
12:30 (demo)
12:55 Asha Rao: nice — question: are these sanitizer prompts editable? we need to ensure they don't leak PII in repair prompts.
13:03 Priya Desai: sanitizer prompts are configurable and you can disable any telemetry; repairs can be run in an isolated environment that doesn't persist prompt history. we'll add a note in the security doc.
13:18 Jordan Kim: last part: pricing model for the pilot — we typically do a time-bound pilot with a consumption estimate and an optional reserved pool for the busiest routes. i'll send a couple of pricing scenarios after the call.
13:33 Mark Li: good.
13:36 Asha Rao: okay wrapping up, any blockers we should call out?
13:40 Diego Fernandez: our legal will want encryption and DPA language up front; ops will want helm manifest and resource estimates.
13:48 Jordan Kim: understood, action items captured. we'll send the security pack, pilot scope, and a short runbook.
13:57 Priya Desai: i'll also share the example schemas and a template for your prompt test-suite so you can run drift checks quickly.
14:08 Asha Rao: thanks both — that was useful.
14:12 Jordan Kim: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs. talk soon.
14:18 (call ends)
